title: Severe Community-Acquired Pneumonia: Severity Assessment and Critical-Care Escalation
specialty: Respiratory Medicine / Infectious Diseases / Emergency Medicine

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) presenting to the emergency department (ED) or acute medical ward: severity assessment with CURB65 and the American Thoracic Society (ATS) and Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) severity criteria, investigations, escalation to critical care, and first-line antibiotics for severe disease. Uses NICE NG250 (2025) and the ATS/IDSA 2019 guideline, with product information for each medicine. Not for hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated pneumonia, aspiration with lung abscess, immunosuppressed patients, tuberculosis, or children.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi adult CAP guideline was found; the pathway follows NICE NG250 and the ATS/IDSA 2019 guideline. The Saudi paediatric CAP guideline and a Jordanian adult aetiology study were found but are not used for adult dosing.

ATS/IDSA recommends covering MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa only where locally validated risk factors exist; no Saudi local resistance data were found, so the add-on branches apply to documented prior isolation, which is the guideline's own sufficient indication.

ATS/IDSA Table 4 says to add anti-pseudomonal cover; piperacillin-tazobactam is a penicillin-class agent, so the pathway gives it in place of the first-line beta-lactam. This substitution is an interpretation, not wording in Table 4.
Levofloxacin dose differs between NICE (500 mg twice daily) and the US label (500 mg or 750 mg every 24 hours); both are shown in the comparison and NICE is used in the pathway.

NICE gives clarithromycin intravenously; the US clarithromycin label opened is for tablets, so intravenous clarithromycin product details (preparation, rate) were not verified; azithromycin intravenous is the verified alternative.
NICE and the ATS/IDSA guideline give no ceftriaxone dose for severe disease within the 1 g to 2 g range; the US label gives 1 g to 2 g once daily, maximum 4 g.
NICE NG250 gives no CAP-specific vancomycin dose (its vancomycin dose is in the hospital-acquired pneumonia table); the ATS/IDSA dose (15 mg/kg every 12 hours, adjusted by levels) is used.

ATS/IDSA 2019 advises against routine corticosteroids in severe CAP and endorses the Surviving Sepsis Campaign for refractory septic shock; the Surviving Sepsis Campaign document was not opened, so no corticosteroid dose is given.
Typical adult laboratory reference ranges are not taken from the guidelines; laboratories differ.

pathophysiology.summary: Community-acquired pneumonia is an acute lung infection acquired outside hospital; severity usually corresponds to risk of death (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.2.8). Severe CAP is defined by the ATS/IDSA 2007 criteria: one major or three or more minor criteria (ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 1). Major criteria are septic shock needing vasopressors or respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation (ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 1). Delayed or inadequate empiric antibiotics carry a much greater risk in severe CAP (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 11 rationale). Prior respiratory isolation of MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the previous year predicts a high risk of these pathogens (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 11 rationale).

symptoms: Acute cough, breathlessness, fever and pleuritic chest pain (NICE NG250, Section 1.2).
Confusion or new disorientation (NICE NG250, Box 2).
Features of sepsis or cardiorespiratory failure (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.2.7).
physicalSigns: Respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute or more (NICE NG250, Box 2).
Low blood pressure: systolic below 90 mmHg or diastolic 60 mmHg or less (NICE NG250, Box 2).
Hypothermia (core temperature below 36 degrees Celsius) and multilobar infiltrates (ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 1).
Hypoxaemia: ratio of arterial oxygen to inspired oxygen (PaO2/FiO2) of 250 or less (ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 1).
redFlags: Septic shock needing vasopressors or respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation: direct admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 7).
CURB65 score of 3 to 5: more than 15% mortality risk; inpatient care with referral to critical care if appropriate (NICE NG250, Box 2 and Recommendation 1.2.9).
Three or more ATS/IDSA minor criteria (ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 1).
Suspected sepsis: follow the NICE sepsis guideline (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.5.3).
Prior respiratory MRSA or Pseudomonas isolation (ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 4).
precipitants: Age 65 years or more (NICE NG250, Box 2).
Comorbidity, frailty or pregnancy affecting the severity score (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.2.9).
Recent hospitalisation with parenteral antibiotics in the last 90 days raises resistance risk (ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 4).
Prior MRSA or Pseudomonas isolation (ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 4).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Lung ultrasound can help when an alternative diagnosis such as heart failure is possible (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.4.2).
Lung ultrasound helps investigate pleural complications (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.4.2).
Test a respiratory sample for influenza in season; severe influenza pneumonia does not routinely get corticosteroids (ATS/IDSA 2019, Questions 4 and 12).
Test urinary Legionella antigen in severe CAP (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 3).
Do not routinely add anaerobic cover unless lung abscess or empyema is suspected (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 10).

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Diagnose, including chest X-ray, within 4 hours of presentation to hospital (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.4.1); multilobar infiltrates is an ATS/IDSA minor criterion (ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 1).

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise severity and resuscitate
actions: Assess airway, breathing and circulation; if sepsis is suspected follow the NICE sepsis guideline (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.5.3).
Score CURB65 and check the ATS/IDSA criteria (NICE NG250, Box 2; ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 1).
Send blood cultures and a respiratory sample before antibiotics when severe (ATS/IDSA 2019, Questions 1 and 2).

clinicalManagement.title: Give antibiotics
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within 4 hours of presentation, sooner if sepsis
actions: Give intravenous combination therapy: a beta-lactam plus a macrolide (see medicines) (NICE NG250, Table 1; ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 4).
Use levofloxacin if penicillin allergy; add MRSA or Pseudomonas cover only for documented prior isolation or locally validated risk (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 11).
Review intravenous antibiotics by 48 hours and switch to oral when possible (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.5.5).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate to critical care
actions: Admit directly to the intensive care unit (ICU) for hypotension requiring vasopressors or respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 7).
Use the minor criteria with clinical judgement to decide on higher levels of care (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 7).
CURB65 of 3 or more needs inpatient care with referral to critical care if appropriate (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.2.9).

clinicalManagement.title: Complete the work-up
actions: Chest X-ray within 4 hours, baseline C-reactive protein, and urinary antigens (NICE NG250, Recommendations 1.4.1, 1.4.3 and 1.4.6; ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 3).
Test for influenza in season (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 4).
Do not routinely give corticosteroids in severe CAP (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 12).

clinicalManagement.title: Set the antibiotic course
actions: Narrow the antibiotic to the culture result when available (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.5.6).
Stop after 5 days unless results suggest longer or the patient is not clinically stable (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.6.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge
actions: Discharge when the patient is clinically stable; consider early discharge to a virtual ward or hospital at home if improving but needing monitoring (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.2.10).
Arrange follow-up chest imaging only if indicated (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 16).

regimens.indication: Empiric treatment of severe community-acquired pneumonia
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with severe CAP, no penicillin allergy
regimens.genericName: Co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin with clavulanic acid) 1000 mg/200 mg powder for injection
regimens.dose: 1.2 g (1000 mg amoxicillin with 200 mg clavulanic acid) intravenously three times a day (NICE NG250, Table 1; Augmentin SPC and leaflet: every 8 hours). Preparation: dissolve one 1000 mg/200 mg vial in 20 mL Water for Injections (about 20.9 mL) and use or dilute within 20 minutes; for infusion add to 100 mL infusion fluid. Give by slow injection over 3 to 4 minutes or infusion over 30 to 40 minutes (Augmentin SPC, Section 4.2 and leaflet Section 7).
regimens.duration: 5 days unless microbiology or instability requires longer (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.6.3); review at 48 hours for oral switch
adjustments: Creatinine clearance (CrCl) above 30 mL/min: no change; 10 to 30 mL/min: 1000 mg/200 mg then 500 mg/100 mg twice daily; below 10 mL/min: 1000 mg/200 mg then 500 mg/100 mg every 24 hours (Augmentin SPC, Section 4.2).
Hepatic impairment: dose with caution and monitor liver function (Augmentin SPC, Section 4.2).
Elderly: no adjustment (Augmentin SPC, Section 4.2).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Liver function and renal function (Augmentin SPC, Section 4.4).
Rash, anaphylaxis and diarrhoea (Augmentin SPC, Section 4.4).
Clinical stability at 48 hours (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.5.5).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to any penicillin (Augmentin SPC, Section 4.3).
Previous severe immediate reaction to another beta-lactam (Augmentin SPC, Section 4.3).
History of jaundice or hepatic impairment due to amoxicillin with clavulanic acid (Augmentin SPC, Section 4.3).

regimens.indication: Empiric treatment of severe community-acquired pneumonia
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with severe CAP, no penicillin allergy
regimens.genericName: Ceftriaxone 1 g and 2 g powder for injection
regimens.dose: 1 g to 2 g intravenously once daily (ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 4 footnote); usual adult daily dose 1 g to 2 g once daily, maximum 4 g per day (Ceftriaxone label, Section Dosage and Administration). Preparation: reconstitute and give as a 30-minute infusion; do not use calcium-containing diluents such as Ringer's or Hartmann's solution (Ceftriaxone label, Section Dosage and Administration and Section Pharmacokinetics).
regimens.duration: 5 days unless microbiology or instability requires longer (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.6.3)
adjustments: Renal or hepatic impairment alone: no adjustment; with both, limit to 2 g daily (Ceftriaxone label, Section Dosage and Administration).
Elderly: no adjustment (Ceftriaxone label, Section Geriatric Use).

monitoring: Rash and hypersensitivity (Ceftriaxone label, Section Warnings).
Diarrhoea suggesting Clostridioides difficile infection (Ceftriaxone label, Section Warnings).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to ceftriaxone or any cephalosporin (Ceftriaxone label, Section Contraindications).
Neonates requiring calcium-containing intravenous solutions, and hyperbilirubinaemic neonates (Ceftriaxone label, Section Contraindications).
Intravenous solutions containing lidocaine (Ceftriaxone label, Section Contraindications).

regimens.dose: 500 mg twice a day orally or intravenously (NICE NG250, Table 1; ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 4 footnote). Tablet strengths 250 mg and 500 mg (Clarithromycin label, Section Dosage Forms and Strengths). Intravenous preparation was not verified.
regimens.duration: 5 days unless microbiology or instability requires longer (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.6.3)

Reduce the dose by 50% with atazanavir or ritonavir-containing regimens (Clarithromycin label, Section 2.7).
Check for interacting drugs before use, including colchicine, simvastatin and lovastatin (Clarithromycin label, Section 4).

regimens.indication: Atypical pathogen cover in severe community-acquired pneumonia
regimens.dose: 500 mg intravenously once daily for at least 2 days, then 500 mg orally once daily to complete 7 to 10 days (Azithromycin label, Section 2.1); ATS/IDSA 2019 Table 4 footnote lists azithromycin 500 mg daily. Preparation: add 4.8 mL Sterile Water for Injection to the 500 mg vial (100 mg/mL), then dilute to 1 mg/mL or 2 mg/mL. Infuse 1 mg/mL over 3 hours or 2 mg/mL over 1 hour; never as a bolus or intramuscularly (Azithromycin label, Section 2.2).
regimens.duration: At least 2 days intravenous, 7 to 10 days total on the label; NICE advises stopping at 5 days unless unstable
adjustments: Torsades de pointes risk with QT prolongation: use caution in patients with long QT, hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia (Azithromycin label, Section 5).
Severe hepatotoxicity reported: stop if hepatitis symptoms appear (Azithromycin label, Section 5).
May worsen myasthenia gravis (Azithromycin label, Section 5).

monitoring: QT interval on an electrocardiogram (ECG) in at-risk patients (Azithromycin label, Section 5).
Liver function (Azithromycin label, Section 5).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to azithromycin, erythromycin, any macrolide or ketolide (Azithromycin label, Section 4.1).
History of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction with prior azithromycin use (Azithromycin label, Section 4.2).

regimens.patientGroup: Adults with severe CAP and prior MRSA
regimens.dose: 15 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours, adjusted by serum levels (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 11 and Table 4 footnote); NICE NG250 hospital-acquired pneumonia table gives 15 mg/kg to 20 mg/kg two or three times a day, loading dose 25 mg/kg to 30 mg/kg in seriously ill people, maximum 2 g per dose (NICE NG250, Table 3). diagnosticCriteria.threshold: One point each: confusion, urea over 7 mmol/L, respiratory rate 30 or more, systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 mmHg or less, age 65 or more; 0 to 1 low risk (under 3%), 2 intermediate (3% to 15%), 3 to 5 high (over 15%) (NICE NG250, Box 2).
As CURB65 without urea; 0 low (under 1%), 1 or 2 intermediate (1% to 10%), 3 or 4 high (over 10%) (NICE NG250, Box 1).

One major criterion (septic shock needing vasopressors; respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation) or three or more minor criteria (respiratory rate 30 or more; PaO2/FiO2 250 or less; multilobar infiltrates; confusion; urea nitrogen 20 mg/dL or more; white cell count below 4000/microlitre; platelets below 100,000/microlitre; core temperature below 36 degrees Celsius; hypotension needing aggressive fluid resuscitation) (ATS/IDSA 2019, Table 1).
Hypotension requiring vasopressors or respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 7; strong recommendation).
Start as soon as possible after diagnosis and within 4 hours of presentation to hospital (NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.5.1).

teaching.scope: Adults with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) presenting to the emergency department (ED) or acute medical ward: severity assessment with CURB65 and the American Thoracic Society (ATS) and Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) severity criteria, investigations, escalation to critical care, and first-line antibiotics for severe disease. Uses NICE NG250 (2025) and the ATS/IDSA 2019 guideline, with product information for each medicine. Not for hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated pneumonia, aspiration with lung abscess, immunosuppressed patients, tuberculosis, or children.
learningObjectives: Stratify severity with CURB65 and the ATS/IDSA criteria.
Start combination antibiotics within 4 hours and sooner with sepsis.
Admit directly to ICU for vasopressor or ventilator need.
Add MRSA or Pseudomonas cover only for documented risk.
pitfalls: Delaying antibiotics for imaging or cultures.
Missing a drug interaction with clarithromycin.
Treating beyond 5 days without a reason.
keyPoints: Severe CAP is one major or three or more minor criteria.
A beta-lactam plus a macrolide is the standard severe regimen.
Review intravenous antibiotics by 48 hours and stop at 5 days if stable.
Corticosteroids are not routine in severe CAP.

patientEducation: Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs; severe pneumonia needs hospital and sometimes intensive care.
Take or receive every antibiotic dose; tell the team if you have a penicillin allergy.
Stop smoking and ask about pneumonia and influenza vaccines.
Return if breathing, fever or confusion worsens after discharge.
lifestyleAndDiet: Rest and drink fluids during recovery.
Ask your doctor about pneumococcal and influenza vaccination.
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician; respiratory physician; intensive care team; microbiologist or infectious diseases physician; clinical pharmacist; physiotherapist; nursing team.
dischargeCriteria: Clinically stable (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure and oxygen saturation within the thresholds in NICE NG250 Recommendation 1.6.3); oral antibiotics arranged to complete 5 days; follow-up and vaccination discussed.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review in primary care after discharge; safety-net advice; consider follow-up chest imaging only when indicated (ATS/IDSA 2019, Question 16; NICE NG250, Recommendation 1.2.9).
